continuation.rootDivergence: What if the Bering land bridge never flooded?

path.title: Reindeer Herders Cross Continents
path.summary: Permanent land allows Siberian reindeer herding, sled design, and cold-climate clothing techniques to spread gradually into Alaska by foot and caravan. Northern communities on both sides develop a shared seasonal round, exchanging breeding animals and knowledge each year.

changes.assumption: Curated illustration for this saved story: the Bering land connection remains exposed.
changes.uncertainty: The painted connection is schematic; its extent and coastline are not reconstructed.

path.title: Herders Map Interior River Routes
path.summary: Reindeer sled teams extend seasonal travel inland, producing route maps of Alaskan rivers, passes, and shelter sites shared among northern communities. This exploration is possible because reliable herds, sled designs, and cold-climate clothing from the cross-Beringian exchange reduce the risks of long winter journeys.
path.causalLink: The established cross-continental seasonal round created dependable herds, staging pastures, and guide knowledge that could be extended from coastal Beringia into Alaska's interior.

path.title: Sled Teams Reach Great Slave Lake
path.summary: Guided by the mapped Yukon and Tanana corridors, reindeer caravans reach the Mackenzie basin and Great Slave Lake, recording portages and winter pastures along the way. The journey follows from the parent maps because staged shelter sites and dependable herds turn a previously uncertain interior crossing into a repeatable seasonal route.
path.causalLink: The Fairbanks river-route maps, shelter lists, and staging herds provide the navigational chain and resupply points needed to extend travel eastward into the Mackenzie basin.
